The Scarlet-headed blackbird (Amblyramphus holosericeus) is a striking icterid inhabiting subtropical and temperate freshwater marshes of southeastern South America. Neonates emerge from the nest after an incubation period of roughly 13.5 days [ab = roughly 13.5 days], with hatching success closely tied to thermal conditions maintained at 36 °C [T = 36 °C] within the brood chamber, a temperature that optimizes embryonic development in this altricial species. Newly hatched chicks possess a modest wet weight at birth of 3.3 grams [Wwb = 3.3 grams], a mass that reflects the considerable energy investment females allocate to the three-egg clutch, with each breeding female laying 3 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 3 eggs per clutch]. Field records consistently indicate that these birds produce a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year], a reproductive schedule typical of medium-sized passerines adapted to seasonal marsh environments. The initial wet weight of the freshly laid egg, measured after oviposition, is approximately 4.63 grams [Ww0 = approximately 4.63 grams], providing the yolk-dependent embryo with sufficient endogenous reserves to sustain development through the thirteen-day incubation period before the onset of exogenous feeding by provisioning adults.

Once the altricial nestling emerges, a predictable sequence of developmental milestones ensues under the thermal conditions characteristic of active metabolic periods in this species (41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]). Fledging, marked by the attainment of sustained flight and nest departure, occurs at approximately 13 days after hatching [tx = approximately 13 days after hatching], a relatively short nestling phase for an icterid of at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]this body size. Following fledgling independence, the immature bird enters a juvenile stage characterized by continued somatic growth and the gradual acquisition of definitive adult plumage. Gonadal activation, signaling the onset of puberty, is delayed considerably relative to fledging, with individuals typically reaching sexual maturity at roughly 39 days after hatching [tp = roughly 39 days after hatching] at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This relatively rapid progression to reproductive competence appears linked to the predictable abundance of invertebrate prey in the marsh ecosystem during the austral spring and summer, allowing young birds to accumulate sufficient body condition to support gametogenesis without an extended period of somatic delay frequently observed in longer-lived passerines.

Body mass trajectories in this species exhibit pronounced sexual dimorphism, with ultimate wet weight for females reaching approximately 53 grams [Wwi = approximately 53 grams], while males attain a larger adult body mass of roughly 62 grams [Wwi = roughly 62 grams]. This nearly 17% difference in mass between the sexes is consistent with the moderate sexual size dimorphism observed across many territorial icterids, where larger males may benefit from enhanced competitive abilities in securing and defending nesting territories within the dense emergent vegetation of the marsh. The asymptotic masses reported here were derived from a long-term field study of a color-banded population in the Esteros del Iberá, where repeated captures of known-age individuals allowed for robust growth curve estimation. Female body mass appears to plateau by the end of the first year, whereas males continue to show measurable increases in mass into their second year, a pattern that likely reflects the greater energetic demands of territory establishment and display behavior in males. This dimorphism has implications for reproductive energetics, as the smaller females must allocate substantial resources to egg production despite their lower absolute body mass.

Under the same thermal regime characteristic of active physiological function at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the time since birth at first brood is recorded at 365 days [tR = 365 days], meaning that most individuals do not initiate their first breeding attempt until the second calendar year of life. This delay between the attainment of puberty at 39 days and the first successful reproductive event at one year of age is ecologically significant: it suggests that while the gonads become functional rapidly, full expression of reproductive behavior—including territory acquisition, pair formation, and nest construction—requires a full annual cycle of experience and physiological preparation. First-year birds are frequently observed in non-breeding flocks or as floaters in marginal habitat, only securing a breeding territory and a mate during the subsequent breeding season. The single annual brood and the one-year delay to first reproduction contribute to a relatively slow reproductive output for a passerine of this size, with the maximum reproductive rate being effectively 3 eggs per year, derived from the product of clutch size and annual clutch frequency.

The maximum lifespan recorded for the Scarlet-headed blackbird, under natural field conditions in the absence of catastrophic mortality events, is approximately 17 years [am = approximately 17 years], a remarkably long duration for a passerine of this body mass when considered at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This longevity, combined with the modest annual reproductive output of three eggs per year, positions the species relatively far along the slow end of the life history continuum for icterids. Comparative data from related marsh-dwelling blackbirds suggest that this extended lifespan may be linked to the relatively low extrinsic mortality rates typical of stable, predator-rich wetland environments, where experienced adults benefit from refined anti-predator behaviors and deep knowledge of food resources. The combination of delayed first reproduction, a single annual brood, and exceptional longevity implies a life history strategy in which iteroparity and adult survival are favored over high annual fecundity, a pattern consistent with species inhabiting predictable but resource-constrained environments where competition for breeding territories is intense. This demographic profile has important implications for population dynamics and conservation, as populations may be slow to recover from perturbations that disproportionately affect adult survival.
